title: 2  Study population and sampling
text:
2.1 Sampling procedure
The GIFT study began with a patient inception cohort survey (PIC Survey) from which we determined eligibility for the clinical intervention trial. Georgia and California SEER registry leads at Emory University and University of Southern California identified an inception cohort of eligible patients (via Information Management Services Calverton MD Katz et al. (2025)) aged 18 and older, diagnosed with a broad array of cancers in 2018-2019, who linked (via the ongoing Georgia California Genetic Testing Linkage Initiative Katz et al. (2025)) to germline testing, and who were found to have a pathogenic variant (PV) in one of 27 cancer susceptibility genes and were alive at the time of selection (n=4300).
Supplemental Table 1 lists the genes included in the study, grouped by cancer susceptibility and guidelines for prevention and control at the time of selection of the patient sample.(Daly et al. (2021)) The SEER registries provided a third-party honest broker, Information Management Services, Inc. (IMS; the honest broker for the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Surveillance Program), with the de-identified clinical datasets maintained by the registries from the Georgia California Genetic Testing Linkage Initiative. IMS sampled an inception cohort of patients from this file using both clinical and genetic test result data according to the study eligibility criteria. IMS “salted” the sample with an additional 5% patients who did not link to a test result, which ensured that registry field teams did not know whether a given patient was tested or not, nor the result of any genetic test. After salting, IMS returned the patient IDs of the sampled individuals to the respective registry, with no information regarding genetic test status. Inclusion criteria for the Patient Inception Cohort (PIC) survey and subsequent invitation to the trial were given in the main text.

title: 5  Interventions
text:
The website guided patients through features of the intervention platform. Each feature was presented, and the patient was able to choose how deeply to engage with each one. Features available to patients in all four study arms included: 1) Key facts and education about genetics, cancer risk, and the role of genetic counseling and testing for families with a history of cancer; 2) The ability to invite family members via personalized email to join the study and receive genetic testing via our test partner, Color Health (Burlingame, CA); and 3) A study “dashboard” that gave enrolled patients the ability to monitor their progress inviting relatives into the study and review communication tips and strategies to follow-up with their relatives. Patients randomized to Study Arms 3 and 4 also had direct access to the Stanford Family Health Navigator, via phone, email, and/or video conference supported by the clinical cancer genetics research site based at Stanford University. The Navigator could help them use the website, answer questions, invite family members to participate in the study and follow up with patients proactively to encourage them to complete study tasks.
Patient (cluster) intervention: Enrolled patients had access to the online GIFT Study website for up to 6 months and could access it as many times as they wanted. The website collected information from patients about their health and their family and was lightly tailored based on information provided by the patients on the PIC survey (e.g., “You told us you have three sisters”).
Relative intervention: For the relative-level intervention, relatives first completed a brief eligibility screener. Enrolled relatives were guided through an online baseline survey to collect information needed to tailor their intervention experience and were then given access to the online GIFT Study website for a total of six months. As for the patient participants, the website guided enrolled relatives with the intervention platform, with each feature presented and the relative able to choose how deeply to engage with each one. Features available to relatives in all four study arms included: 1) Key facts and education about genetics and how it relates to cancer risk, the different types of genetic test results and their meaning, and privacy regarding genetic test results; 2) An exercise designed to help them consider their reasons for getting genetic testing (including commonly endorsed motivational and hesitation statements); 3) A brief description of the Color Health genetic testing process and the ability to follow a unique link to order free ($0) or low-cost ($50) genetic testing from Color (according to their study arm) in the first 90 days only; and 4) The ability to consent to share the fact that they have enrolled in the study with the patient who invited them to join.
The study website contained a link to the Color website that embedded a unique Color token directly in the URL; it indicated that they were enrolled in the GIFT Study and the charge to the relative participant for their genetic test ($50 vs free). No study participant personal identifiable or health information was shared with Color. Relatives who clicked the link to order genetic testing followed Color’s standard procedures for ordering a genetic test, which included informed consent for the testing procedure. Relatives in family clusters randomized to Study Arms 3 and 4 had access to the Family Health Navigator, via phone/email/ videoconference (as described above for the patient intervention). Details of the Data Monitoring and Collection procedures have been published elsewhere.(Katz et al. (2025))

title: 8  Testing - Primary
text:
8.2 Summary of primary outcome results
The cost arm shows a significant improvement in testing with an odds ratio of 2.5 and a difference in probability of 4% (95% CI 2%,5%) when in the control condition for Navigation and averaged over number of relatives, family communication and gender of the relative. The estimate of 4% increase is in line with the 3% increase that we hypothesized for our sample size calculation.
The navigation intervention arm is not significantly different from 0 and the 95% confidence interval for the differnce of 0% is -1% to 2%, which does not include the 5% difference we hypothesized for our sample size calculation
The residual ICC at 0.41 is larger than what we expected (0.15). The baseline predictors female and number of relatives were strongly predictive of testing while the index patient’s baseline comfort with communication scale was not. We pre-specified the use of these variables in the protocol to improve the efficiency of our estimation as it has been shown that this can improve balance and efficiency in cluster randomized trials(Hemming et al. (2025)).

12.0.3 Distribution of random effects for testing
Generalized multilevel models also make an assumption of normally distributed random effects.
For testing, given the descriptive data showing substantial numbers of people with 0 testing we suspect the assumption is moderately violated.

As expected there is departure from normality at the lower end of the random effects scale. title: 14  Numerator and deonominators
text:
14.1 Testing outcome
Reviewers requested numbers and percentages (numerators and denominators) of eligible and tested.
We had described already in the paper that there were 4946 total eligible relatives across the four arms of the study of whom 948 were invited and 267 were tested.
We chose a cluster randomized design with adjustment for baseline covariates based on a clinical conceptual framework focused on patients and their families and attention to precision of measuring causal effects. The causal effects for this design are estimated by predicted probabilities of testing and invitation conditional on covariate values that isolate the comparison of interest. Given the complexity of the design, it is not possible to present simple numerators and denominators the way it might be for a multi-arm, non-cluster randomized clinical trial with no baseline covariates.
However, we can present the unadjusted proportions which are quite similar to the full model proportions.

text:
15.1 Rationale for not examining interactions
During the review process a reviewer requested that we provide an analysis of the interaction between the two interventions, free vs low cost and navigator vs no navigator and we provide that analysis below. We had not planned to conduct this analysis for reasons outlined first.

title: 15  Intervention interactions
text:
15.1.1 Lack of prior belief in a mechanism of interaction
In carrying out the primary analysis for the main trial results we committed ourselves to follow the protocol as pre-specified and previously published (PMID: 40016666). There we provide the following justification following the Consort extensions for factorial trials which specifies that “For trials in which evaluation of interaction(s) is not deemed essential, this decision should be justified.” (item-17a, PMID: 38051324):
Our justification, as pre-specified in the protocol paper (Katz et al. (2025)), was given as follows:

“First, we do not hypothesize that there will be any synergistic effect of the two treatments on the log odds scale and thus assume that the effects will be additive. Conceptually we cannot think of any reason that the effect of the cost of the testing and any help provided by a navigator over the website have an obvious reason to be dependent on the level of the other. Thus, our primary outcome for the primary and secondary aims is the treatment effect of each intervention in a regression model without an interaction term.”



15.1.2 Inadequate power and risk of type 2, type M and type S errors

True interaction effect size was anticipated to be small during trial design

We did not anticipate any synergism between the two interactions which would result in an effect size close to 0.
Factorial designs are often employed for the increased efficiency that occurs in the absence of interactions between factors and this is often justified by invoking the “hierarchical ordering principle” which says that lower order effects (such as main effects) tend to be more important than higher order effects. There are both theoretical and empirical justifications for this principle.(Wu and Hamada (2011), Li, Sudarsanam, and Frey (2006), Montgomery (2013)) This gives rise to a common default in the absence of prior information or strong theory of proposing that interactions effects are about half the magnitude of main effects when designing experiments.



Interaction terms require 16 times the sample size as main effects
If the true interaction effect is zero or close to it, as we hypothesized, then the sample size for detecting an interaction would increase toward infinity as the true effect approached 0. If, as an upper limit, one hypothesizes an interaction effect that is half the size of a main effect, then the sample size required to detect a statistically significant difference is 16 times the sample size that is required to detect a main effect (see this source for a description of how you would calculate this). Given the difficulty of achieving sample sizes sufficient to detect main effects in most clinical trials, interaction effects are likely to almost always be severely under-powered.


There are risks of estimating underpowered effects
The obvious risk of estimating effects when the sample size is too small is that a type 2 error occurs and you accept the null hypothesis when it is not true. However recent work has shown 2 additional errors that can occur which have been given the names of type M and type S errors (Gelman and Carlin (2014);van Zwet, Schwab, and Senn (2021)) A type M error is an exaggeration error, the risk that with an inadequate sample size and a small true effect, that in a given sample from the population a statistically signficant result will be exaggerated relative to the true effect size. A type S error is the risk of a reversal of the sign of the observed effect with respect to the true effect.
The magnitude of these errors can be calculated using an R package called retrodesign. (Timm A (2024). retrodesign: Tools for Type S (Sign) and Type M (Magnitude) Errors. R package version 0.2.2, https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=retrodesign.)


Main effect specified in design (coefficient) 0.53 (o.r. 1.7 ) 


True intervention effect 0.27 (half of main effect) 


Observed interaction standard error 0.49

The design analysis shows the power to detect the interaction is 0.07 and the type M error is 4.4 (based on the observed standard error for the interaction from the interaction analysis below and the upper limit of the likely true effect size). This suggests that if one observed a statistically significant effect it would be on average over four times as large as the true effect. There is a 7% chance that the sign would be in the opposite direction to the true effect.
We can also run a simulation to illustrate the problem directly.


code
retrodesign::sim_plot(true_interaction_effect,std_error_interaction)









We see that under the conditions of low power to detect the interaction, the majority of data samples which might be declared signficicant due to a type 1 error would be severely exaggerated relative to the proposed true effect.
However, more recent articles about how to present results of factorial trials do tend to suggest that the interaction analysis should be included as a sensitivity analysis even when there is inadequate sample size and the interaction is not anticipated. This recommendation occurs even when some of the authors acknowledge the risk of exaggeration errors discussed below. The rationale seems to be that it is more transparent, allows readers to make their own decisions and that appropriate cautions about over-interpretation can be given along side the interaction analysis.

title: 15  Intervention interactions
text:
15.3 Interpretation
Some researchers label attempts to interpret analyses for which the sample size is inadequate as “story time” (see Gelman 2010), others label it more optimistically as “hypothesis generating interpretation”. Whichever label one might lean toward, it is difficult to try to interpret these results which we feel is a result of the fact that they likely represent noise.

15.3.1 Invitation model
Looking at the invitation model where the interaction is “statistically signficant”, neither intervention increases invitation (stable invite proportion 20-22%) but patients exposed to the navigator in the control cost arm have a lower invitation proportion.

If we accept that the interaction is real then the interpretation would have to explain what the navigator did that discouraged patients from inviting relatives when the testing cost was $50 (low-cost), but had no effect on invitation when the testing was free as compared to both cost arms with no navigator.

We might postulate that the navigator 1) found out about which patients were in the higher cost arm, and 2) out of concern for the costs to the relatives somehow encouraged the patients to invite fewer relatives maybe focusing on those for whom testing might be higher yield. The navigator was blinded to cost but possibly could have asked or been told by the patient in conversation.
However, an invitation also would have allowed the relative to access useful information decision support and about testing which was designed to be of value even if they decided not to test for financial or other reasons, and the navigator was trained to emphasize this.

In addition navigator role was to help with navigating the process of testing and giving advice on how to talk to relatives. The navigator had no professional expertise in genetics and was not able to offer opinions about the specific usefulness or lack of usefulness of of testing in specific relatives under cost constraints. So it is difficult to accept this mechanism or to come up with another for this finding.
Finally, only 1/3 of patients assigned to the navigator arm actually spoke with the navigator (78/203) so any effect of the navigator would be diluted making it even more difficult to explain how the navigator could have had this effect when averaged over all the patients randomized to this arm.

The other interpretation is that the interaction null hypothesis is true, there is no differential effect of the navigator across groups and the observed interaction coefficient is a “false positive” signficant result or type I error. Furthermore it is exaggerated in magnitude due to magnification bias or type M error described above.



15.3.2 Testing model
If one accepts that the navigator decreased invitations but only when paired with the low-cost ($50) control intervention arm, then one might also be tempted to interpret the testing model with the interaction as suggesting that there is a modest net positive effect of the navigator once relatives are invited.

In this story, the Navigator:low-cost arm, despite a lower invitation rate, is observed to have similar testing rates to the No-navigator:low-cost control arm. This then implies that the navigator exposure increases the conversion of invited relatives to tested relatives relative to the conversion that occurs in the absence of a navigator.
Similarly the point effect in the Navigator:free-test arm is modestly higher than the free-test only arm when they had similar invitation rates. This again might suggest that the navigator exposure increases the conversion of invited relatives to tested relatives.

There are two reasons to be cautious with this interpretation of point estimates.

First, the confidence intervals of the four arms in the testing model substantially overlap other than the contrast represented by the marginal effect of free-test (third and fourth rows in the graph) vs low-cost test (first two rows in the graph).

Second, inferences about proportion tested once invited is a form of simplistic mediation analysis which is a non-randomized comparison. Invitation to testing occurs after randomization and the invitation to testing is not randomly assigned to relatives within family. At best one could do an observational formal mediation analysis which would require adjustment for a number of potential confounders, as in any observational analysis, as opposed to the randomized comparisons we present where balance of all confounders can be assumed.

For these reasons, and in consideration of the cautions described above, we would not try to draw conclusions about the interaction analysis based on this data or even interpret the findings as hypothesis generating given the lack of precision in the estimates and that we are unable to come up with a plausible mechanism by which the invitation results could occur.
